topics.description: The software layer that manages hardware and provides services to programs, so applications need not address devices directly.
The core of the OS. It schedules the CPU, manages memory, drives devices, and enforces permissions. Everything else is userspace.
Privileged kernel execution versus unprivileged application execution. The boundary is what stops one program corrupting another.
The controlled entry point by which a userspace program asks the kernel to do privileged work such as opening a file.
The program interpreting typed commands and turning them into process execution. Bash is the common default.
The interface presenting a shell. The terminal displays; the shell interprets. They are routinely conflated.
The Unix design principle by which devices, sockets, and kernel state are all reached through the filesystem interface.
Linux runs many users and many processes concurrently, isolating each — which is why permissions and process ownership exist at all.
The kernel packaged with GNU tools, a package manager, defaults, and a release policy. The kernel alone is not a usable system.
Debian family (Debian, Ubuntu, Mint) using .deb and apt; Red Hat family (RHEL, Fedora, CentOS Stream, Rocky) using .rpm and dnf; SUSE; Arch.
topics.notes: Knowing which package manager belongs to which family is commonly tested.

topics.description: Long-term-support releases freeze versions and backport fixes for years; rolling releases ship continuously. Stability against currency.
Linux is the kernel; most of the surrounding userland is GNU. This is why the combination is sometimes called GNU/Linux.
Begun by Linus Torvalds in 1991 as a free Unix-like kernel, developed openly ever since and now governed under the Linux Foundation.
Linux is Unix-like and largely POSIX-conformant, which is why skills and scripts port across Unix systems.
The kernel is released under GPLv2, which is why distributions may redistribute and modify it under the same terms.
Executes instructions. Core count and architecture determine how much work runs genuinely in parallel.
Volatile working memory. When it is exhausted the system swaps to disk and slows sharply, or begins killing processes.
Persistent block devices — HDD, SSD, NVMe — that hold filesystems and survive power loss.
x86_64 and ARM64 are the common ones. Binaries and container images are architecture-specific.
Kernel code that drives hardware, loadable at runtime as modules rather than compiled in.
Low-level software embedded in a device, distinct from the operating system that runs above it.
Graphical and command-line interfaces. Servers are usually administered by CLI because it is scriptable, remotable, and cheap in resources.
GNOME, KDE Plasma, XFCE and others provide the graphical desktop; the choice is independent of the distribution.
The display server protocols underlying Linux graphics, Wayland being the newer replacement. Recognition-level.
Named values inherited by processes, configuring behaviour without changing code.
The ordered list of directories the shell searches for commands. Explains "command not found" for an installed program.
topics.notes: A very common cause of confusing command-not-found errors.

topics.description: Identifying what a machine is: kernel version, distribution, hostname, uptime, architecture.
A command, its options (flags), and its arguments. Short options take one dash, long options two.
Man pages, --help, apropos, and info. Man pages have numbered sections; section 5 covers file formats, which is where config syntax lives.
topics.notes: Knowing man sections exist, and that section 5 documents file formats, is worth having.

topics.description: An absolute path starts at / and is unambiguous; a relative path is interpreted from the current directory.
Current directory, parent directory, and the current user’s home.
Moving around and listing contents, including hidden dotfiles which ls omits by default.

path: creating and removing files and directories
topics.description: touch, mkdir, cp, mv, rm. rm is immediate and unrecoverable; there is no recycle bin.
topics.notes: rm -rf with a wrong path is the classic catastrophic mistake.

topics.description: cat for short files, less for paging, head and tail for the ends, tail -f to follow a growing log.
find walks the tree live and filters on name, size, time, or permission; locate queries a prebuilt index and is faster but can be stale.
The shell expands * ? and [] into matching filenames before the command ever runs.
topics.notes: Expansion happens in the shell, not the command — which is why quoting changes behaviour.

topics.description: Double quotes preserve spacing but still expand variables; single quotes suppress all expansion; a backslash escapes one character.
topics.notes: Unquoted variables containing spaces are a frequent scripting bug.

topics.description: stdin, stdout and stderr — file descriptors 0, 1 and 2. Errors travel separately from output, which is why 2> exists.
> writes to a file and truncates it, >> appends, < reads from a file, 2> captures errors, and /dev/null discards.
topics.notes: > silently destroys the existing contents of the target file.

topics.description: Connects one command’s stdout to the next command’s stdin, letting small tools be composed. stderr is not carried by default.
; runs sequentially regardless, && runs only on success, || runs only on failure.
Substitutes a command’s output into another command, written $(...).
Variables are local to the shell until exported, at which point child processes inherit them.
Recalling previous commands and completing names, both of which reduce typing errors.
Short names for longer commands, defined in shell startup files.
Searches input for lines matching a pattern. The single most-used text tool on a Linux system.
topics.notes: grep searches inside files; find locates files. A commonly confused pair.

topics.description: Pattern syntax used by grep, sed, and others. Basic anchors, character classes and quantifiers are enough at this level.
Stream editor, most often used for search-and-replace across a file or pipeline.
Field-aware text processor, natural for columnar output such as printing the third column of a report.
Extract fields, order lines, collapse duplicates, and count. uniq only collapses adjacent duplicates, so sort usually precedes it.
topics.notes: uniq without a preceding sort is a classic mistake.

topics.description: Shows differences between files, the basis of patches and code review.
vi/vim is present on essentially every Unix system; nano is simpler. Knowing how to save and quit vi is a practical necessity.
topics.notes: Being trapped in vi is a rite of passage; :q! exits without saving.

topics.description: tar bundles many files into one archive; gzip, bzip2 and xz compress. tar czf creates a compressed archive in one step.
Moving files between hosts with scp, sftp, or rsync; rsync transfers only differences and can resume.
A file of commands made executable, beginning with a shebang naming the interpreter.
Conditionals and loops — if, for, while — plus positional parameters for arguments.
Determining what a file actually is and when it changed, rather than trusting its extension.
